questions.e: Each choice is made in turn, so by the multiplication principle there are 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 sandwiches. Adding the choices (4 + 3 + 2 = 9) would count picking one item from any group, not one from each group.

questions.s: How many three-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if no digit may be repeated?
questions.e: There are 5 choices for the hundreds digit, then 4 for the tens and 3 for the units: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. 125 = 5³ allows repetition, and 10 = C(5, 3) only chooses the digits without arranging them.

questions.s: Let C(n, r) be the number of ways to choose r objects from n different objects. What is the value of C(8, 3) + C(8, 4)?
questions.e: C(8, 3) = 56 and C(8, 4) = 70, so the sum is 126; this agrees with Pascal's rule C(8, 3) + C(8, 4) = C(9, 4) = 126. Choosing 84 = C(9, 3) uses the wrong lower index in Pascal's rule.

questions.s: A class of 10 students must choose 2 representatives with equal roles. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.e: The order does not matter, so the number is C(10, 2) = (10 × 9)/2 = 45. The value 90 = 10 × 9 counts each pair twice, as if the two roles were different.

questions.s: Six people, including Ahmed and Li Wei, stand in a row. In how many arrangements do Ahmed and Li Wei stand next to each other?
questions.e: Treat Ahmed and Li Wei as one block: the block and the other 4 people give 5 units, arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Inside the block the two can swap, so the total is 2 × 120 = 240. Answering 120 forgets the internal order of the pair.

questions.s: Six people, including Amina and Carlos, stand in a row. In how many arrangements are Amina and Carlos NOT next to each other?
questions.e: All arrangements: 6! = 720. Arrangements with the two together: 2 × 5! = 240. So the number with them apart is 720 − 240 = 480. The option 240 is the number of arrangements where they are together.

questions.s: A lock code has 3 characters, and each character is one of the digits 0 to 9. Digits may be repeated. How many different codes are possible?
questions.e: Each of the 3 positions has 10 choices, so there are 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 codes (000 to 999). 720 = 10 × 9 × 8 wrongly forbids repetition, and 999 forgets the code 000.

questions.s: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can the committee contain exactly 2 boys?
questions.e: Choose 2 of the 5 boys and 1 of the 4 girls: C(5, 2) × C(4, 1) = 10 × 4 = 40. 84 = C(9, 3) is the number of all committees, with no condition on the boys.

questions.s: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can the committee contain at least one girl?
questions.e: Use the complement: all committees C(9, 3) = 84 minus all-boy committees C(5, 3) = 10 gives 74. Subtracting the all-girl committees C(4, 3) = 4 instead gives the wrong value 80.

questions.s: How many different arrangements of the letters of the word BANANA are there?
questions.e: BANANA has 6 letters with A repeated 3 times and N repeated 2 times, so the count is 6!/(3! × 2!) = 720/12 = 60. 120 = 6!/3! only allows for the repeated A's and forgets the two N's.

questions.s: How many diagonals does a convex octagon (8 sides) have?
questions.e: Any 2 of the 8 vertices give C(8, 2) = 28 segments; 8 of these are sides, so there are 28 − 8 = 20 diagonals. 28 forgets to remove the sides.

questions.s: Using the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with no digit repeated, how many four-digit even numbers can be formed?
questions.e: Last digit 0: the other three places take 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 ways. Last digit 2 or 4: the first digit cannot be 0 or the last digit, so 4 choices, then 4 × 3 for the middle: 2 × 48 = 96. Total 60 + 96 = 156. The value 96 forgets the numbers ending in 0, and 180 ignores that 0 cannot lead.

questions.s: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability that the number shown is a prime number?
questions.e: The primes among 1 to 6 are 2, 3 and 5, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2. Counting 1 as a prime gives the wrong value 4/6 = 2/3; 1 is not prime.

questions.s: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue and 3 green balls of the same size. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is blue or green?
questions.e: There are 3 + 3 = 6 blue or green balls out of 10, so the probability is 6/10 = 3/5. The value 2/5 is the probability of red, the complement.

questions.s: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is 8?
questions.e: Among 36 equally likely ordered outcomes, sum 8 comes from (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2): 5 outcomes, so 5/36. Counting only unordered pairs {2,6}, {3,5}, {4,4} gives 3/36 = 1/12, but those pairs are not equally likely.

questions.s: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is at least 10?
questions.e: Sum 10: 3 outcomes, sum 11: 2 outcomes, sum 12: 1 outcome, total 6 of 36, so 6/36 = 1/6. The value 1/12 = 3/36 counts only sums 11 and 12, forgetting the sum 10.

questions.s: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
questions.e: There are 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes, and exactly 2 heads occurs in HHT, HTH, THH: 3 outcomes, so 3/8. The value 1/4 wrongly treats the 4 possible numbers of heads (0, 1, 2, 3) as equally likely.

questions.s: Two cards are drawn at the same time from six cards numbered 1 to 6. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is even?
questions.e: The product is odd only if both cards are odd: C(3, 2) = 3 of C(6, 2) = 15 pairs. So P(even) = 1 − 3/15 = 4/5. The value 1/5 is the probability of an odd product.

questions.s: Three boys and two girls stand in a row in random order. What is the probability that the two girls stand at the two ends?
questions.e: The girls occupy 2 of the 5 places, and all C(5, 2) = 10 pairs of places are equally likely; only one pair is the two ends, so the probability is 1/10. Equivalently 2! × 3!/5! = 12/120. The value 2/5 is only the probability that one particular girl stands at an end.

questions.s: An integer is chosen at random from 1 to 20. What is the probability that it is divisible by 3 or by 5?
questions.e: Multiples of 3: 6 numbers; multiples of 5: 4 numbers; 15 is in both lists. So 6 + 4 − 1 = 9 numbers and the probability is 9/20. Adding 6 + 4 = 10 to get 1/2 counts 15 twice.

questions.s: Which of the following values can be the probability of an event?
questions.e: Any probability P satisfies 0 ≤ P ≤ 1, and only 0.75 lies in this interval. A negative value such as −0.2 and values above 1 such as 4/3 and 1.05 are impossible.

questions.s: The probability that event A happens is 0.35. What is the probability that A does not happen?
questions.e: Complementary events have probabilities adding to 1, so P(not A) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. The value 1.35 adds instead of subtracting and is greater than 1, which is impossible.

questions.s: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A ∪ B), the probability that at least one of them happens?
questions.e: Independence gives P(A ∩ B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2, so P(A ∪ B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7. The value 0.9 simply adds the probabilities, which is only correct for mutually exclusive events.

questions.s: Three players shoot at a target independently. Their probabilities of hitting it are 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4. What is the probability that the target is hit at least once?
questions.e: All three miss with probability (1/2)(2/3)(3/4) = 1/4, so at least one hit has probability 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The value 1/4 is the probability that everyone misses, and 1/24 is the probability that all three hit.

questions.s: Each time Fatima attempts a puzzle she solves it with probability 0.6, independently of other attempts. What is the probability that she solves it for the first time on her third attempt?
questions.e: She must fail twice and then succeed: 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.096. The value 0.144 = 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.4 swaps the roles of success and failure.

questions.s: What is the mean of the data 16, 2, 9, 18, 5?
questions.e: The sum is 16 + 2 + 9 + 18 + 5 = 50, and 50/5 = 10. The value 9 is the median (middle value of 2, 5, 9, 16, 18), not the mean.

questions.s: What is the median of the data 12, 5, 8, 20, 15, 9?
questions.e: In order the data are 5, 8, 9, 12, 15, 20; with 6 values the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (9 + 12)/2 = 10.5. Taking the middle pair of the unsorted list, (8 + 20)/2 = 14, forgets to sort first.

questions.s: What is the mode of the data 4, 6, 6, 7, 9, 9, 9, 10?
questions.e: The mode is the most frequent value; 9 appears three times, more than any other value. The mean is 60/8 = 7.5 and the median is (7 + 9)/2 = 8, so those options answer different questions.

questions.s: The mean of five numbers is 12. Four of the numbers are 10, 14, 8 and 15. What is the fifth number?
questions.e: The total of the five numbers is 5 × 12 = 60, and the four known numbers add to 47, so the fifth is 60 − 47 = 13. Guessing 12 assumes the missing number equals the mean, which is not required.

questions.s: The data x₁, x₂, …, xₙ have mean 5 and variance 4. What are the mean and the variance of the data 3x₁ + 2, 3x₂ + 2, …, 3xₙ + 2?
questions.e: For y = ax + b the mean becomes a·x̄ + b = 3 × 5 + 2 = 17 and the variance becomes a² × 4 = 9 × 4 = 36. Adding 2 does not change the spread, so 14 = 3 × 4 + 2 is wrong, and 12 forgets to square the factor 3.

questions.s: Using s² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², what is the variance of the data 2, 4, 6, 8, 10?
questions.e: The mean is 6, and the squared deviations are 16, 4, 0, 4, 16 with sum 40, so s² = 40/5 = 8. Dividing by n − 1 = 4 gives 10, which is not the formula stated. 2√2 is the standard deviation.

questions.s: Using s² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², what is the standard deviation of the data 1, 3, 5, 7?
questions.e: The mean is 4; squared deviations 9, 1, 1, 9 add to 20, so the variance is 20/4 = 5 and the standard deviation is √5. The option 5 is the variance, not its square root.

questions.s: The number 10 is added to every value in a data set. Which of the following stays the same?
questions.e: Shifting every value by 10 moves the whole data set without changing how far the values are from each other, so the standard deviation is unchanged. The mean, median and mode all increase by 10.

questions.s: The table shows the scores of 20 students on a 5-point task. What is the mean score?
questions.e: The total score is 1×2 + 2×5 + 3×8 + 4×3 + 5×2 = 2 + 10 + 24 + 12 + 10 = 58, so the mean is 58/20 = 2.9. The value 3 is the median and the mode, not the mean.

questions.s: The table shows how many books each of 25 students read last month. What is the median number of books?
questions.e: With 25 values the median is the 13th. The cumulative frequencies are 3, 11, 17, …, so the 12th to 17th values are 2 and the median is 2. The value 1 is the mode (the largest frequency, 8), not the median.

questions.s: Ten numbers x₁, …, x₁₀ have mean 6 and variance 2, where the variance is (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)². What is the value of x₁² + x₂² + … + x₁₀²?
questions.e: Variance = (Σx²)/n − x̄², so Σx² = n(s² + x̄²) = 10 × (2 + 36) = 380. The value 362 adds the variance only once instead of multiplying it by n.

questions.s: Class A has 30 students with mean mark 70, and class B has 20 students with mean mark 80. What is the mean mark of all 50 students?
questions.e: Total marks: 30 × 70 + 20 × 80 = 2100 + 1600 = 3700, so the mean is 3700/50 = 74. The simple average (70 + 80)/2 = 75 ignores that class A is larger.

questions.s: The data 6, 8, x, 10, 12 have mean 9. Using s² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², what is the standard deviation of the data?
questions.e: From 36 + x = 45 we get x = 9. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 0, 1, 9 with sum 20, so s² = 20/5 = 4 and s = 2. The value 4 is the variance; √5 comes from dividing by n − 1.

questions.s: What is the range of the data 15, 7, 22, 9, 18?
questions.e: Range = largest − smallest = 22 − 7 = 15. The value 13 = 22 − 9 wrongly uses the second smallest value.

questions.s: Four numbers have mean 10. After a fifth number is added, the mean of the five numbers is 11. What is the fifth number?
questions.e: The first four numbers total 4 × 10 = 40 and the five numbers total 5 × 11 = 55, so the fifth is 55 − 40 = 15. Answering 11 assumes the new number equals the new mean.

questions.s: A data set has standard deviation 3. Every value is multiplied by −2. What is the standard deviation of the new data?
questions.e: For y = ax the standard deviation becomes |a| × 3 = 2 × 3 = 6 (the variance becomes 4 × 9 = 36). A standard deviation is never negative, so −6 is impossible.

questions.s: Which statement about the data 3, 4, 4, 5, 104 is correct?
o: The mean is 24 and the median is 4
The mean is 4 and the median is 24
The mean is 24 and the median is 5
The mean is 23 and the median is 4
questions.e: The sum is 120, so the mean is 120/5 = 24, while the middle value of the ordered data is 4. The single large value 104 pulls the mean up but does not change the median, which is why the two are so different.

questions.s: The table shows the number of children in each of 40 families. What is the mean number of children per family?
questions.e: Total children: 0×6 + 1×12 + 2×14 + 3×6 + 4×2 = 66, so the mean is 66/40 = 1.65. The value 2 is the median and the mode of this table, not the mean.

questions.s: Five numbers have mean 6 and variance 2, where variance is (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)². The number 6 is added to the data. What is the variance of the six numbers?
questions.e: The mean stays 6, and the sum of squared deviations stays 5 × 2 = 10 because the new value has deviation 0. The new variance is 10/6 = 5/3. Answering 2 forgets that n has increased to 6.

questions.s: The heights of 20 plants are grouped in the table. Using the midpoint of each class, estimate the mean height.
questions.e: Midpoints are 155, 165 and 175, so the estimate is (155×4 + 165×10 + 175×6)/20 = (620 + 1650 + 1050)/20 = 3320/20 = 166 cm. 165 cm is only the midpoint of the modal class, not the mean.

questions.s: The table shows the marks of a group of students; one frequency x is missing. The mean mark is 6.5. What is x?
questions.e: Total marks 15 + 6x + 35 + 16 = 66 + 6x and number of students 10 + x, so 66 + 6x = 6.5(10 + x) = 65 + 6.5x, giving 0.5x = 1 and x = 2. Check: 78/12 = 6.5. Forgetting to add x to the number of students gives a wrong equation.

questions.s: The standard deviation of a data set is 0. Which statement must be true?
questions.e: A standard deviation of 0 means every squared deviation (xᵢ − x̄)² is 0, so every value equals the mean. The values need not be 0: the data 5, 5, 5 have standard deviation 0 and mean 5.

questions.s: Data set A is 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and data set B is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Which statement is correct?
o: Same mean; A has the larger variance
Same mean; B has the larger variance
questions.e: Both sets have mean 6. The variance of A is (4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4)/5 = 2 and of B is (16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16)/5 = 8, since B is A's deviations doubled. So B is more spread out.

questions.s: The mean age of six friends is 15 years. When Kwame joins the group, the mean age of the seven friends becomes 16 years. How old is Kwame?
questions.e: The six friends total 6 × 15 = 90 years and the seven total 7 × 16 = 112 years, so Kwame is 112 − 90 = 22. Answering 16 assumes his age equals the new mean.

questions.s: The data 1, 2, 3, x, y have mean 3 and variance 2, where variance is (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)². What is the value of xy?
questions.e: From the mean, x + y = 9. From the variance, 4 + 1 + 0 + (x − 3)² + (y − 3)² = 10, so with u = x − 3, v = y − 3: u + v = 3 and u² + v² = 5, giving uv = 2, so {u, v} = {1, 2} and {x, y} = {4, 5}. Hence xy = 20. Treating the variance sum as 2 instead of 5 × 2 = 10 leads to no real solution.

questions.s: A random variable X follows the normal distribution N(50, σ²). What is P(X < 50)?
questions.e: The normal curve is symmetric about the mean μ = 50, so exactly half of the probability lies below 50: P(X < 50) = 0.5. The value 0.68 is the probability of lying within one standard deviation of the mean, which is a different interval.

questions.s: X follows the normal distribution N(10, σ²) and P(X > 13) = 0.2. What is P(7 < X < 10)?
questions.e: By symmetry about 10, P(7 < X < 10) = P(10 < X < 13) = P(X > 10) − P(X > 13) = 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.3. The value 0.6 is P(7 < X < 13), the whole interval on both sides of the mean.

questions.s: X follows a normal distribution N(μ, σ²) with P(X < 2) = P(X > 8). What is μ?
questions.e: Equal tail probabilities mean that 2 and 8 are symmetric about the mean, so μ = (2 + 8)/2 = 5. The value 10 adds the two numbers without halving.

questions.s: Test scores X follow N(100, 15²). Use P(μ − σ < X < μ + σ) ≈ 0.68. What is P(X > 115), approximately?
questions.e: 115 = μ + σ. Outside (85, 115) the probability is 1 − 0.68 = 0.32, split equally between the two tails, so P(X > 115) ≈ 0.16. The value 0.32 forgets to halve for one tail only.

questions.s: X follows N(60, 5²). Use P(μ − σ < X < μ + σ) ≈ 0.68 and P(μ − 2σ < X < μ + 2σ) ≈ 0.95. What is P(55 < X < 70), approximately?
questions.e: 55 = μ − σ and 70 = μ + 2σ. By symmetry P(55 < X < 60) ≈ 0.68/2 = 0.34 and P(60 < X < 70) ≈ 0.95/2 = 0.475, so the total is about 0.815. Choosing 0.68 or 0.95 treats the interval as symmetric about the mean, which it is not.

questions.s: Which statement about the probability density curve of the normal distribution N(μ, σ²) is correct?
o: Its highest point is at x = σ
The total area under the curve is 2
A larger σ makes the curve taller and narrower
It is symmetric about the line x = μ
questions.e: The normal curve is symmetric about x = μ and its highest point is at x = μ. The total area under any probability density curve is 1, and a larger σ makes the curve flatter and wider, not taller.

questions.s: The scores of 1000 students follow N(70, 10²) approximately. Use P(μ − 2σ < X < μ + 2σ) ≈ 0.95. About how many students scored above 90?
questions.e: 90 = μ + 2σ, and the probability outside (50, 90) is 1 − 0.95 = 0.05, half in each tail, so P(X > 90) ≈ 0.025 and about 0.025 × 1000 = 25 students. The value 50 forgets to split the 0.05 between the two tails.

questions.s: X follows N(1, σ²) and P(X < −1) = 0.1. What is P(|X − 1| < 2)?
questions.e: |X − 1| < 2 means −1 < X < 3. By symmetry about 1, P(X > 3) = P(X < −1) = 0.1, so the probability is 1 − 0.1 − 0.1 = 0.8. The value 0.9 subtracts only one tail.

questions.s: A device has two parts that work independently. Part A works with probability 0.9 and part B with probability 0.8. The device works only if both parts work. What is the probability that the device works?
questions.e: For independent events, P(A and B) = 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72. The value 0.98 = 1 − 0.1 × 0.2 is the probability that at least one part works, which would be the answer if either part were enough.

questions.s: Two independent alarms protect a shop. They work with probabilities 0.7 and 0.6. What is the probability that at least one alarm works?
questions.e: Both fail with probability 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12, so at least one works with probability 1 − 0.12 = 0.88. The value 0.42 = 0.7 × 0.6 is the probability that both work.

questions.s: Amina and Carlos try to solve a problem independently. Amina solves it with probability 1/3 and Carlos with probability 1/4. What is the probability that exactly one of them solves it?
questions.e: P(only Amina) = 1/3 × 3/4 = 3/12 and P(only Carlos) = 2/3 × 1/4 = 2/12, so the total is 5/12. The value 1/2 = 1 − (2/3)(3/4) is the probability that at least one solves it, which also includes both solving it.

questions.s: Li Wei plays a best-of-three match (the first to win 2 games wins). He wins each game with probability 2/3, independently. What is the probability that he wins the match?
questions.e: He wins 2–0 with probability (2/3)² = 4/9, or 2–1 if he loses exactly one of the first two games and wins the third: 2 × (2/3)(1/3)(2/3) = 8/27. Total 12/27 + 8/27 = 20/27. The value 16/27 forgets the factor 2 for the two orders WLW and LWW.

questions.s: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least one tail?
questions.e: The only outcome with no tail is HHHH, with probability (1/2)⁴ = 1/16, so P(at least one tail) = 1 − 1/16 = 15/16. The value 1/16 is the probability of the complement.

questions.s: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that at least one die shows a 6?
questions.e: No six on all three dice has probability (5/6)³ = 125/216, so at least one six has probability 1 − 125/216 = 91/216. Adding 1/6 three times to get 1/2 counts outcomes with two or three sixes more than once.

questions.s: Five students stand in a line. Carlos must not stand at either end. How many arrangements are possible?
questions.e: Carlos takes one of the 3 middle places, and the other 4 students fill the rest in 4! = 24 ways: 3 × 24 = 72. Equivalently 120 − 2 × 24 = 72. The value 96 = 120 − 24 removes only one end.

questions.s: How many subsets (including the empty set and the set itself) does a set with 5 elements have?
questions.e: Each element is either in or out of a subset, giving 2⁵ = 32 subsets by the multiplication principle. The value 31 leaves out the empty set, which is also a subset.

questions.s: There are 10 points in a plane. Exactly 4 of them lie on one straight line, and no other three points are collinear. How many triangles have all three vertices among these points?
questions.e: Any 3 points give C(10, 3) = 120 choices, but the C(4, 3) = 4 choices taken from the collinear points give no triangle. So there are 120 − 4 = 116 triangles. The value 120 forgets the collinear points.

questions.s: In how many ways can 4 different flags be hung in a row on a pole?
questions.e: There are 4 choices for the first place, 3 for the second, 2 for the third and 1 for the last: 4! = 24. The value 256 = 4⁴ allows the same flag to be used more than once.

questions.s: A shelf holds 5 different mathematics books, 4 different physics books and 3 different chemistry books. In how many ways can Kwame choose 2 books from different subjects?
questions.e: Add the three subject pairs: maths–physics 5 × 4 = 20, maths–chemistry 5 × 3 = 15, physics–chemistry 4 × 3 = 12, total 47. The value 66 = C(12, 2) also includes pairs from the same subject.

questions.s: The four letters of the word STAT are arranged in a random order. What is the probability that the two T's are next to each other?
questions.e: There are 4!/2! = 12 different arrangements. Gluing TT into one block leaves 3 objects (TT, S, A) with 3! = 6 arrangements, so the probability is 6/12 = 1/2. The value 1/4 = 6/24 mixes a count of distinct words with 24 arrangements that treat the T's as different.

questions.s: An integer x is chosen at random from 1, 2, …, 10. What is the probability that x² − 5x + 6 ≤ 0?
questions.e: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) ≤ 0 gives 2 ≤ x ≤ 3, so x = 2 or 3 and the probability is 2/10 = 1/5. The value 1/10 counts only one root and forgets that both endpoints satisfy the inequality.

questions.s: Two cards are drawn without replacement from five cards numbered 1 to 5. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is odd?
questions.e: An odd sum needs one odd card (1, 3, 5) and one even card (2, 4): 3 × 2 = 6 of the C(5, 2) = 10 pairs, so the probability is 3/5. The value 2/5 is the probability of an even sum.

questions.s: Three guests each choose one of 3 rooms at random, independently of each other. What is the probability that all three guests choose different rooms?
questions.e: There are 3³ = 27 equally likely choices, and the number with all rooms different is 3! = 6, so the probability is 6/27 = 2/9. The value 1/9 = 3/27 is the probability that all three choose the same room.

questions.s: A spinner has 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. What is the probability that one spin lands on a number greater than 5?
questions.e: The numbers greater than 5 are 6, 7 and 8, so the probability is 3/8. The value 5/8 is the probability of a number 5 or less.

questions.s: Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8. The value 0.65 = 0.8 − 0.15 wrongly uses the independence formula P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 × 0.5.

questions.s: X follows N(μ, σ²) with P(X < 4) = 0.3 and P(X > 10) = 0.3. What is P(4 < X < μ)?
questions.e: Equal tails at 4 and 10 give μ = 7. Then P(4 < X < 10) = 1 − 0.3 − 0.3 = 0.4, and by symmetry P(4 < X < 7) is half of it, 0.2. The value 0.4 is the whole interval from 4 to 10.

questions.s: Six different books are shared among three students, Ahmed, Amina and Kwame, so that each student gets exactly 2 books. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.e: Ahmed's 2 books can be chosen in C(6, 2) = 15 ways, Amina's in C(4, 2) = 6 ways and Kwame takes the last 2: 15 × 6 = 90. The value 15 = 90/3! counts only the splits into three unnamed pairs, but here the students are different.

questions.s: Which of the following is a measure of how spread out a data set is?
questions.e: The standard deviation measures how far the values typically lie from the mean, so it describes spread. The mean, median and mode are measures of the centre (average) of the data.

questions.s: Three students are chosen at random from 4 boys and 3 girls. What is the probability that the group contains at least one boy and at least one girl?
questions.e: There are C(7, 3) = 35 groups. All-boy groups: C(4, 3) = 4; all-girl groups: C(3, 3) = 1. So the probability is 1 − 5/35 = 6/7. A common slip is to remove only the all-boy groups, which gives 31/35 instead.

questions.s: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability that both show heads?
questions.e: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT, and only HH gives two heads, so the probability is 1/4. The value 1/3 treats 'two heads, one of each, two tails' as equally likely, but 'one of each' happens in two ways.

questions.s: A restaurant menu has 3 starters and 5 main courses. A meal is one starter and one main course. How many different meals are possible?
questions.e: By the multiplication principle there are 3 × 5 = 15 meals. Adding 3 + 5 = 8 would count choosing one dish only, and 30 counts each meal twice.

questions.s: One letter is chosen at random from the 10 letters of the word STATISTICS. What is the probability that it is S or T?
questions.e: STATISTICS contains 3 S's and 3 T's, so 6 of the 10 letters are S or T and the probability is 6/10 = 3/5. The value 3/10 counts only one of the two letters.

questions.s: What is the mean of the data 6, 8, 13, 17?
questions.e: The sum is 6 + 8 + 13 + 17 = 44, and 44/4 = 11. The value 10.5 = (8 + 13)/2 is the median, not the mean.

questions.s: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability that it does not show a 6?
questions.e: P(not 6) = 1 − P(6) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6, since the faces 1 to 5 are the favourable outcomes. The value 1/6 is the probability of the event itself, not its complement.

questions.s: Eight runners take part in a race. In how many ways can the gold and silver medals be awarded (no ties)?
questions.e: Gold can go to any of 8 runners and silver to any of the remaining 7, so there are 8 × 7 = 56 ways. The value 28 = C(8, 2) ignores that gold and silver are different medals.

questions.s: A team of 4 is chosen from 6 men and 5 women. In how many ways can the team have exactly 2 men and 2 women?
questions.e: Choose the men in C(6, 2) = 15 ways and the women in C(5, 2) = 10 ways; multiply: 15 × 10 = 150. Adding 15 + 10 = 25 is wrong because each choice of men goes with every choice of women, and 330 = C(11, 4) ignores the condition.

questions.s: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is odd?
questions.e: The product is odd only when both numbers are odd: 3 × 3 = 9 of the 36 outcomes, so the probability is 9/36 = 1/4. The value 1/2 is the probability that one given die is odd, not both.

questions.s: Using s² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², what is the variance of the data 5, 6, 8, 9, 12?
questions.e: The mean is 40/5 = 8; the squared deviations are 9, 4, 0, 1, 16 with sum 30, so s² = 30/5 = 6. Dividing by 4 instead gives 7.5, and √6 is the standard deviation.

questions.s: The table shows the quiz scores of 20 students. Which statement is correct?
questions.e: The largest frequency is 7, for score 9, so the mode is 9. The median is the mean of the 10th and 11th scores; cumulative frequencies 1, 5, 11 show both are 8, so the median is 8. Taking 8.5 assumes the middle pair falls in different classes.

questions.s: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.3. What is the probability that neither A nor B happens?
questions.e: The complements are also independent, so P(neither) = (1 − 0.6)(1 − 0.3) = 0.4 × 0.7 = 0.28. The value 0.1 = 1 − 0.6 − 0.3 wrongly treats A and B as mutually exclusive.

questions.s: X follows N(80, σ²) and P(X > 90) = 0.15. What is P(X < 90)?
questions.e: X < 90 is the complement of X > 90 (for a continuous variable P(X = 90) = 0), so P(X < 90) = 1 − 0.15 = 0.85. The value 0.70 is P(70 < X < 90), which uses symmetry about 80 but is a different interval.

questions.s: Which pair of events is independent?
o: Taking two balls from a bag without putting the first back
Tossing a coin and then rolling a die
Getting an even number and a 2 on one roll of a die
Rain today and the ground being wet today
questions.e: The coin result has no effect on the die, so these events are independent. Drawing without replacement changes the second draw, rolling a 2 already guarantees an even number, and rain makes wet ground more likely, so those pairs are dependent.

questions.s: In how many ways can 5 people sit around a round table, if only their positions relative to each other matter?
questions.e: Fix one person's seat to remove rotations; the other 4 people can then be arranged in 4! = 24 ways. The value 120 = 5! counts each seating 5 times, once for each rotation.

questions.s: Two cards are drawn at the same time from six cards numbered 1 to 6. What is the probability that the two numbers add up to 7?
questions.e: The pairs with sum 7 are {1,6}, {2,5}, {3,4}: 3 of the C(6, 2) = 15 pairs, so the probability is 3/15 = 1/5. Using 15 pairs is essential; 1/6 (the dice answer) would wrongly allow the same card twice.

questions.s: The mean of 8 numbers is 15. One of the numbers, 22, is removed. What is the mean of the remaining 7 numbers?
questions.e: The 8 numbers total 8 × 15 = 120, so the remaining 7 total 120 − 22 = 98 and their mean is 98/7 = 14. Removing a value above the mean must lower the mean, so 15 and 16 cannot be right.

questions.s: What is the median of the data 3, 9, 4, 8, 1, 7, 6?
questions.e: Sorted, the data are 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, and the middle (4th) value is 6. The value 8 is the middle of the unsorted list, which is not the median.

questions.s: A bag has 3 red and 2 white balls. Two balls are drawn at the same time. What is the probability that at least one is white?
questions.e: Both red has probability C(3, 2)/C(5, 2) = 3/10, so at least one white has probability 1 − 3/10 = 7/10. The value 3/5 = 6/10 counts only exactly one white and leaves out the pair of two whites.

questions.s: A data set has mean 20 and standard deviation 4. Each value x is changed to 0.5x − 3. What are the new mean and standard deviation?
questions.e: The mean becomes 0.5 × 20 − 3 = 7 and the standard deviation becomes |0.5| × 4 = 2; subtracting 3 does not change the spread. The value 1 multiplies the standard deviation by 0.5² = 0.25, which is the rule for the variance.

questions.s: How many positive divisors does 72 have?
questions.e: 72 = 2³ × 3², and each divisor is 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ with a ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3} and b ∈ {0, 1, 2}, so there are 4 × 3 = 12 divisors. Multiplying the exponents (3 × 2 = 6) forgets the choice of exponent 0.

questions.s: Four-digit numbers are formed using each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 exactly once. How many of them are greater than 2300?
questions.e: First digit 3 or 4: 2 × 3! = 12 numbers. First digit 2: the second digit must be 3 or 4, giving 2 × 2! = 4 numbers (2314, 2341, 2413, 2431). Total 16. The value 12 forgets the numbers beginning with 2.

questions.s: Two different vertices of a regular hexagon are chosen at random and joined by a segment. What is the probability that the segment is one of the longest diagonals (passing through the centre)?
questions.e: There are C(6, 2) = 15 segments: 6 sides, 6 short diagonals and 3 long diagonals through the centre. So the probability is 3/15 = 1/5. The value 2/5 = 6/15 is the probability of a side (or of a short diagonal).

questions.s: Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.5. What is the probability that neither A nor B happens?
questions.e: P(A ∪ B) = 0.2 + 0.5 = 0.7 because they cannot happen together, so P(neither) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. The value 0.4 = 0.8 × 0.5 wrongly treats the events as independent.

questions.s: Ten numbers x₁, …, x₁₀ have mean 5, and x₁² + x₂² + … + x₁₀² = 290. Using s² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², what is the standard deviation?
questions.e: s² = (Σx²)/n − x̄² = 290/10 − 25 = 29 − 25 = 4, so s = 2. The value 4 is the variance, and √29 forgets to subtract the square of the mean.

questions.s: X follows N(2, σ²) and P(X > a) = P(X < a − 4). What is the value of a?
questions.e: Equal tail probabilities mean a and a − 4 are symmetric about the mean 2, so (a + a − 4)/2 = 2, giving a = 4. Check: P(X > 4) = P(X < 0), and 0 and 4 are each 2 from the mean. Choosing a = 2 puts a itself at the mean, which does not make the tails equal.

questions.s: Five people, including Ahmed and Amina, stand in a row in random order. What is the probability that there is exactly one person between Ahmed and Amina?
questions.e: Ahmed and Amina take an ordered pair of places, 5 × 4 = 20 equally likely choices. Places with exactly one between are (1,3), (2,4), (3,5) in either order: 6 choices, so the probability is 6/20 = 3/10. Counting only 3 of the 20 ordered choices gives 3/20, and other values miscount these pairs.
